doc.title: Chuck Lamb interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, February 7, 2023

chapter: Growing up in Verona and Dry Jack
title: Parents' support and the first drum set
summary: His mother backed his playing, parents were a singer and an artist, he got a drum set at ten and formed The Plastic People with Rich.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Did your parents support your endeavors or did they think — was there ever any talk about getting a real job?

My mom especially was like, when there was talk about me going maybe to music school, actually more it was a reflection back on the time she was like, we talked, “Mom did you ever think of sending Chuck to music school?” And she said, “No, musician, musician. He has to go out and play.” I never —
That’s a very enlightened attitude I think.

Yeah. And my parents were both, well my mom was a singer and she was like in an Andrews Sisters trio with her two sisters in New York City, so that element, and my dad was a very creative artist. But you know they heard, when I was eight or nine, playing, I just had some drum sticks and playing on lampshades and that stuff. Maybe it was to save © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-

the lampshades but they bought me a drum set when I was ten, for a birthday present, from Montgomery Wards, red sparkle Kent. Yes baby. One bass drum, a pole in the middle, one cymbal you know up here. Oh I was in heaven. And then Rich and I started our first band called The Plastic People.

No he played guitar, he played guitar kind of throughout that thing and then when we made the switch, there’s a lot of ancillary roots in these stories of course, but my brother, the next oldest brother, John, was a guitar player and he was playing with us also so there was three brothers. He went to Columbia University and met a drummer, a really great jazz drummer who came back to Verona and then it was like well how about he plays drums and you play piano? It was sort of the start of my — and I said okay. That was just what we did. And we went, “Rich, play bass.” So it was all organically evolving.
